summary:
Gyeonggi Province's region-specific record concerns student protections rather than visitor-facing rules. Gyeonggi-do enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010, and the ordinance bars discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, the clauses that religious groups and parents targeted in the repeal campaign they mounted from August 2022. When the Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished its own ordinance in April 2024, Gyeonggi was one of six regional education offices still enforcing a comparable instrument, together with Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju. A Gyeonggi-based teacher quoted in the coverage argued against wholesale abolition.

Gyeonggi and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances include a right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy. The provincial Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day.

No Gyeonggi-specific rule on criminal exposure, entry, identity documents, airport or security screening, restroom access or healthcare access was identified. Visitors in the province fall under the national framework carried by the South Korea record.
tangentialFactors: The provincial ordinance sits under sustained pressure. The repeal campaign that removed Seoul's version was organised by religious groups and parents objecting to the sexual-orientation clause and was carried by councillors of the ruling People Power Party; the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of what regional councils decided. Whether Gyeonggi's ordinance survives that pressure is the open question for the province's protection framework.
localsOnly: Students in Gyeonggi schools are covered by the provincial student human rights ordinance, including its prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and on pregnancy. The Superintendent of Public Instruction surveys student human rights annually, and the province observes a Student Human Rights Day.
outOfScopeNotes: No Gyeonggi-specific record of complaints, investigations or outcomes under the ordinance's sexual orientation and gender identity clause was found. Whether the ordinance remained in force after April 2024 is not established by the sources. No provincial data on transgender residents' or visitors' experience of policing, healthcare, restroom access or violence was identified.
